proof:
# A parity triangulation bound with a quantitative rank gain

This is a proved arithmetic mass inequality for actual convex fibers.
It is not a center-selection theorem. Its new ingredient is a triangulation
whose volume-root heights are concave, and a tree ascending those heights.
Independent audit is pending.

Let d>=1 and let E be a compact convex subset of R^n times R^d. Choose
a finite nonempty set P of integer bases all in one parity class, with
positive fiber volumes

    w_p=vol_d(E_p),  M_P=sum_(p in P) w_p,  a=max_p w_p.

Write s=dim aff(P), and let M=mu(E) denote its full mixed d-volume.
There is a triangulation graph G on the vertex set P and a maximum-volume
vertex p_* for which

    M >= 2 M_P-a
       +2^(-d)[deg_G(p_*)a
                 +sum_(p!=p_*) (deg_G(p)-2)w_p].     (1)

In particular if s>=2, then

    M >= [2+(s-2)2^(-d)]M_P-(1-2^(1-d))a,           (2)

and therefore

    M-(2M_P-a) >= s 2^(-d)a.                        (3)

Equation(3) follows from the stronger bound
2^(-d)[(s-2)M_P+2a] supplied by(2), since M_P>=a.
The selected P need not contain every positive fiber of its parity class;
unselected fibers are included only in the full mass M. In applications
P can be the entire positive class of any fixed closed oblique cap.

## 1. A concave piecewise-affine interpolation on a triangulation

Put h_p=w_p^(1/d). Whenever p in P is a convex combination of points
of P, convexity of E and ordinary Brunn--Minkowski imply

    h_p >= sum_q alpha_q h_q.

On conv(P) define h(z) as the largest such convex-combination average
with base mean z. Its feasible coefficient set is a compact polytope,
so this maximum exists. Combining feasible representations shows h is
concave; the finite linear program makes it piecewise affine. At every
p in P the preceding inequality and the trivial representation show
h(p)=h_p.

The projected upper faces of conv{(p,h_p):p in P} give a finite polytopal
subdivision on which h is affine. Triangulate that subdivision using a
common pulling order on its vertices, so adjacent faces receive the
same triangulation. Insert any remaining points of P one at a time by
stellar subdivision of the smallest current face whose relative interior
contains that point, and of every simplex containing that face. These
operations add only the prescribed point as a vertex and preserve the
piecewise-affine function h. They produce a triangulation of conv(P)
with vertex set EXACTLY P, on each simplex of which h is affine.

Its graph G has an edge for each one-dimensional simplex. For s>=1
every vertex belongs to an s-dimensional simplex, so deg_G(p)>=s.

## 2. An ascending tree rooted at a maximum

The vertices where h is maximal form a connected subgraph of G. Indeed
the maximum locus of the concave h is convex. In a simplex, its maximum
locus is the face spanned by the maximum-height vertices, or is empty.
These faces triangulate that convex maximum locus, and their graph is
connected. One may verify the last assertion by following a line segment
between vertices through its finite sequence of simplices.

Every nonmaximum vertex p has a neighbor q with h_q>h_p. Take a
maximum-height point z and follow the segment from p toward z. Concavity
makes h strictly greater than h_p at every sufficiently small positive
step. The initial step lies in a simplex containing p; since h is affine
there, some other vertex of that simplex has greater height.

Choose a spanning tree on the connected maximum subgraph and root it at
any p_* there. From every other vertex choose one edge toward a vertex
of strictly greater height. Each ascending path must reach the maximum
subgraph because the graph is finite. Together these edges and the
chosen maximum tree form a spanning tree T directed toward p_*: every
nonroot has one parent, all vertices reach the root, and there are exactly
|P|-1 edges. Along each parent-child edge, the parent's volume is at
least the child's volume.

## 3. Distinct midpoint fibers for the graph edges

For every edge {p,q} of G, the midpoint (p+q)/2 is an integer point,
because the bases have one parity. It is not a vertex of P: the relative
interior of an edge in a triangulation contains no other vertex.
Distinct edges have distinct midpoints because their relative interiors
are disjoint in an embedded simplicial complex. Thus all of these
integer midpoint fibers can be counted separately, also separately
from the source fibers at P. Convexity and fiber Brunn--Minkowski give

    M >= M_P+sum_({p,q} edge of G)
                         ((w_p^(1/d)+w_q^(1/d))/2)^d.         (4)

The statement uses the actual midpoint fiber only once. The distinctness
argument is why a sum over these particular pairs is legitimate, unlike
a sum over all parity pairs without tracking collisions.

Put delta=2^(-d). For parent volume b and child volume c with b>=c>0,
the binomial theorem gives

    ((b^(1/d)+c^(1/d))/2)^d >= delta b+(1-delta)c.    (5)

To check this, all terms other than b in the expansion of the numerator
are at least their binomial coefficient times c; their coefficients sum
to2^d-1. On any other edge the simpler estimate is

    ((w_p^(1/d)+w_q^(1/d))/2)^d >=delta(w_p+w_q).      (6)

Apply(5) to the tree edges and(6) to the other graph edges. The tree
contributes at least

    M_P-a+delta sum_(parent,child in T)(w_parent-w_child).

After adding the remaining edge terms, the coefficient of w_p in the
delta bracket is deg_G(p) at the root, and deg_G(p)-2 elsewhere:
one tree edge leads from a nonroot to its parent, and its child edges
contribute with the opposite sign. Substitution in(4) proves(1).
Using deg_G(p)>=s for s>=2 proves(2) and(3).

## 4. Rank one, sharp limiting calibration, and cap scope

If s=1, the triangulation graph is the path through the ordered P. If
the maximum vertex is an endpoint, the bracket in(1) is a minus the
opposite endpoint volume. If it is internal, the bracket is twice a
minus the sum of the two endpoint volumes. All other vertices have
degree two. Both expressions are nonnegative, because a is the maximum.
For s=0 there is one source fiber and the basic bound M>=a is used
directly; no nonexistent triangulation edges are introduced.

The constant in(3) is attained in the limit by an explicit family. For
s>=2 let E have projection 2 Delta_s and homothetic fibers r(z)K,
where K has volume one and

    r(z)=1-(1-epsilon)(sum_i z_i)/2,  0<epsilon<1.

This positive affine radius defines a convex body. Its all-even class
has one fiber of volume a=1 at zero and s fibers of volume b=epsilon^d
at2e_i. The other bases are e_i, with volume c=((1+epsilon)/2)^d,
and e_i+e_j, with volume b. Hence its exact expansion slack is

    M-(2M_P-a)=s(c-b)+s(s-1)b/2 ->s 2^(-d).

Thus the universal coefficient s2^(-d) in(3) cannot be increased.
This is a sharp mass calibration, not a small-depth example.

Every argument applies verbatim to E=C intersect H for an arbitrary
closed ambient halfspace H with positive selected fiber volumes.
Continuous and integer normal coordinates may be coupled. At a vertical
boundary, the entire boundary fibers remain in E. The proof never changes
the original lattice, rounds a center, or substitutes an integral over
the integer projection. It gives no all-direction center from(1)-(3).

For intrinsic H_q, q>=1, use q in place of d. The direction-space lemma
in `candidate e7b862fa9bf72057`, Section6, makes
the same-parity positive q-fibers parallel. It justifies every anchored
root inequality and every midpoint BM inequality above in their common
q-dimensional direction space. The q=0 case is separate counting and
does not use these root formulas.
